qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

In her State of the Union address, the Commission President stated: ‘When Russia cut us off from gas, we fought back.’ This claim is a political fiction. As recently as 2025, the EU imported 36 billion m³ of gas from Russia, representing approximately 12.5 % of its total imports. Subsequently, the EU itself adopted Regulation (EU) 2026/261, which legally banned the remaining imports of Russian pipeline gas and LNG in accordance with a set timetable. If, therefore, Russia has indeed ‘cut off the EU’s gas supply’, it is strange that the EU was still importing Russian gas as recently as 2025 and that it was the EU itself which adopted the legislation to bring these imports to an end. In light of the foregoing: 1.

Does the Commission consider it appropriate to mislead citizens by claiming that ‘Russia has cut us off from gas’, when the EU was still importing gas from Russia as late as 2025 and subsequently imposed a legal ban on the remaining imports itself?

If the consequences of its own energy decisions can simply be attributed to Russia, does the Commission take the view that the Green Deal, the ETS and the accelerated phaseout of fossil fuels in the EU were also ‘imposed by Russia’?
Is the Commission prepared to take political responsibility for the costs and consequences of its own decisions, or will it continue to shift the blame for its own failures onto external actors?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.11.2026) The Commission is committed to pursue the path towards the EU’s energy transition and to deliver on its climate ambitions and climate neutrality by 2050. At the same time, Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and its choice to selectively cut gas supplies to some Member States highlighted the EU’s exposure to Russia. To stop the weaponisation of energy by Russia and to strengthen the Union’s energy security and independence, the Commission put forward the REPowerEU plan1 with a view to phase out Russian fossil fuel imports, in line with the European Council conclusions of March 2022. Since then, the EU has successfully reduced the share of Russian gas imports from 45% in 2022 to 12% in 2025. Moreover, and as a result of EU sanctions, Russian coal has been eliminated from the EU’s energy mix, and oil imports have declined from 27% at the beginning of 2022 to 2% in 2025. To give effect to the plan, Regulation (EU) 2026/2612 was adopted to establish a prohibition of imports of Russian natural gas. According to the Regulation, all remaining Russian Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) imports will be prohibited as of 1 January 2027 and all remaining Russian pipeline gas imports by 30 September 2027. Addressing both energy crises – the first following Russia’s aggression against Ukraine on 24 February 2022 and the second following the Middle East conflict on 27 February 2026 – reinforces the need to accelerate the clean energy transition, towards affordable and home-grown energy sources.
